faq.q: How does riding with a pillion passenger change motorcycle handling?
faq.a: The bike's centre of gravity shifts upward and rearward, requiring more lean angle for corners, increasing braking distances by 30-40%, and making all inputs feel heavier. You need to adjust suspension preload and ride with smoother, more progressive technique throughout.

faq.q: What suspension adjustments are needed for pillion riding?
faq.a: Increase rear preload to near-maximum settings and slightly increase rebound damping if available. This prevents excessive rear compression under load while maintaining compliance for bumps. Always check your bike's manual for specific two-up settings.

faq.q: How often should I stop when touring with a pillion passenger?
faq.a: Stop every hour to ninety minutes, more frequently than solo riding. Passengers fatigue faster as they're less engaged and more exposed to weather and vibration. Short 15-minute breaks make a significant difference to comfort.

faq.q: What makes a good motorcycle for pillion touring?
faq.a: Look for a proper pillion seat with adequate support, secure grab handles, and accommodation for luggage when the pillion seat is occupied. Adventure bikes and sports tourers typically work best, with comfortable ergonomics for both rider and passenger.

faq.q: Do I need different insurance for carrying pillion passengers?
faq.a: Most UK motorcycle insurance policies automatically cover pillion passengers, but it's worth confirming with your insurer. Ensure your pillion wears proper protective gear and can reach footpegs – this is both a legal and safety requirement.

faq.q: What are the best UK roads for two-up touring?
faq.a: Choose smooth, flowing roads with wide corners rather than tight technical sections. The A82 along Loch Lomond, A591 through the Lake District, and sections of the NC500 work brilliantly for pillion touring, offering good surfaces and spectacular scenery.

content:
Riding Two-Up: Everything You Need to Know About Pillion Touring

I'll be honest with you – the first time I took a pillion passenger on a proper tour, I made every mistake in the book. Set off from Manchester heading up to the Lakes with my mate Dave on the back, and within twenty miles I knew something was wrong. The bike felt different, the braking distances had changed, and Dave was gripping my jacket so hard I thought he'd rip the seams out.

That was years ago, and since then I've logged thousands of miles with pillion passengers across Britain. From the sweeping coastal roads of the NC500 to the tight bends of Snowdonia, I've learned what works and what'll make both of you miserable. Here's everything I wish someone had told me before that first ride.

What Actually Changes When You're Riding Pillion

The physics of your bike transform completely when you add another person. I'm not talking slight differences – I mean everything from acceleration to how you countersteer through corners changes fundamentally. Your bike's centre of gravity shifts upward and rearward, which affects stability more than you'd think.

The first time I took the A537 Cat and Fiddle with a pillion, I nearly ran wide on a corner I'd taken a hundred times solo. The extra weight means you need more lean angle for the same corner speed, and your suspension is working significantly harder. Your rear shock will compress more, potentially bottoming out on bumps that wouldn't trouble you when riding solo.

Braking distances increase by roughly 30-40% depending on your passenger's weight. On wet British roads – and let's face it, that's most of them – this becomes even more critical. I now plan my braking points earlier, especially when descending into places like Bakewell or navigating the tight descents off the Cairngorms.

Suspension Setup Makes or Breaks the Experience

This is non-negotiable. Before you take a pillion on anything more than a quick hop to the shops, you need to adjust your suspension. I learned this the hard way bombing down the A82 alongside Loch Lomond with completely inappropriate settings. The bike wallowed through corners and the rear end felt vague and unsettled.

Most modern bikes have easily adjustable preload on the rear shock. Wind it up for pillion use – check your bike's manual for specific settings, but you're typically looking at near-maximum preload. If your bike has rebound damping adjustment, increase that slightly too. The goal is to prevent the rear end compressing excessively under load while keeping the suspension compliant enough to absorb our brilliant British potholes.

Front preload might need attention too, though this is less common. Some riders increase it by a click or two to balance the bike's pitch. If you're doing serious touring with a pillion, consider upgrading to a quality aftermarket rear shock. I fitted a Nitron to my bike three years ago and the difference for two-up touring is night and day.

Choosing the Right Bike for Pillion Work

Not all bikes are created equal when it comes to carrying passengers. I've ridden pillion on sportsbikes where I felt like I was clinging to a slippery torpedo, and I've taken passengers on adventure bikes where they had acres of space and proper grab handles.

Look for bikes with a proper pillion seat – not an afterthought postage stamp bolted onto the tail. Your passenger needs actual support, not just a perch that'll leave them sliding into you under braking. Grab handles are essential. If your bike doesn't have them, fit some. Your passenger hanging onto your jacket or shoulders throws off your balance and makes precise control difficult.

Adventure bikes and tourers are naturally suited to pillion work. I run a BMW GS for serious two-up touring, and the comfort level for passengers is excellent. Sports tourers like the Kawasaki Versys or Yamaha Tracer hit a sweet spot between performance and passenger comfort. Even some nakeds work well – the Yamaha MT-09 Tracer I borrowed last summer proved surprisingly good for two-up rides through the Yorkshire Dales.

Luggage Considerations

When you're carrying a pillion, your luggage options shrink. That massive tail bag you normally strap on? Forget it – that's where your passenger sits. You're looking at panniers, tank bags, or a top box.

I run hard luggage from SportsBikeShop for all my two-up tours. Soft luggage can work, but make sure it's properly secured and doesn't restrict your pillion's leg position. Nothing ruins a tour faster than your passenger getting cramp because a pannier's digging into their calf.

Keep the weight distribution balanced. I pack heavy items low and central, lighter stuff in the top box if I'm running one. Check out my packing checklist for specific guidance on what to bring and where to stow it.

Communication: The Make or Break Factor

Here's something nobody talks about enough – you need a way to communicate. Hand signals work for basics, but trying to explain "I'm pulling over because I think I heard something weird from the engine" via taps on the shoulder is useless.

I invested in a Bluetooth intercom system four years ago and it transformed pillion riding. Being able to chat, warn about upcoming hazards, or just share the experience makes touring together genuinely enjoyable rather than isolating. Your passenger can tell you if they need a break before they're desperately uncomfortable, and you can explain your riding decisions.

Brief your pillion before you set off, even if they've ridden with you before. I always cover the basics: stay still during slow speed manoeuvres, don't lean in opposition to the bike in corners (just follow my body position), keep feet on pegs at all stops, and communicate if anything feels wrong.

The difference between a good pillion experience and a nightmare often comes down to communication and comfort breaks. Take them more frequently than you think necessary.

Riding Technique Adjustments for Two-Up

Everything becomes smoother and more deliberate when you're carrying a passenger. Those quick inputs that work solo need to be smoothed out. I treat the throttle, brakes, and steering like I'm transporting a cup of hot tea on the tank – no sudden movements.

Acceleration needs to be progressive. Crack the throttle open too quickly and your passenger's weight shifts back, compressing the rear suspension and potentially upsetting the bike's balance. I've seen pillions nearly slide off the back when riders grab a handful of throttle at traffic lights. Smooth and steady wins here.

Braking requires early planning. I start braking significantly earlier than I would solo, using progressive pressure rather than sharp grabs. Engine braking becomes your friend – I downshift earlier and use the engine to scrub speed before touching the brakes. On descents like the drop into Keswick from Whinlatter Pass, this technique prevents brake fade and keeps things comfortable.

Cornering With a Passenger

This is where it gets interesting. The extra weight means you need more lean angle for the same corner speed, but you also need to be smoother getting there. I used to rush my corner entries – that doesn't work with a pillion.

Set your speed earlier, get your braking done in a straight line, then smoothly roll the bike into the corner. The extra weight actually helps mid-corner stability once you're settled, but quick direction changes feel heavier and slower. Riding the NC500 two-up taught me to read the road further ahead and plan my lines more carefully.

Your passenger's position matters too. They should look over your shoulder in the direction of the turn, naturally following your body position. A passenger who fights the lean or sits rigidly upright makes the bike harder to steer and less stable.

Comfort and Rest Stops

Passengers get tired faster than riders. You're engaged with the bike, constantly active with inputs and reading the road. Your pillion is just sitting there trying to stay comfortable while being buffeted by wind and absorbing every bump.

I stop every hour to ninety minutes when touring two-up, more frequently than my usual two-hour solo schedule. These don't need to be long breaks – fifteen minutes to stretch legs, have a drink, and reset makes all the difference. The Scottish Highlands have brilliant stopping points with views that make breaks a pleasure rather than a chore.

Invest in proper gear for your passenger. A quality helmet with good ventilation, a waterproof jacket and trousers (this is Britain, remember), and proper gloves are essential. I keep a spare set of heated grips attachments for really cold days – cold hands and feet turn passengers miserable fast.

British Weather Considerations

Passengers suffer more from weather than riders. You've got the screen and the fairing to break the wind and rain; they're more exposed. I fitted a larger touring screen to my bike specifically for pillion work, and the difference in passenger comfort is substantial.

In rain, your pillion gets soaked faster. Waterproofs need to be genuinely waterproof, not just shower-resistant. I learned this crossing the Pennines in a downpour with a passenger in "water-resistant" gear. By the time we reached the other side, they were saturated and freezing.

Cold is the bigger enemy though. Wind chill affects passengers more severely. I carry spare neck warmers and ensure my pillion has layers. On winter rides through the Peak District or when heading up to the Island to Highlands route, thermal layers aren't optional – they're essential.

Insurance and Legal Considerations

Quick reminder because I've seen people overlook this – check your insurance covers pillion passengers. Most policies do, but it's worth confirming, especially if you're taking paying passengers or doing it commercially.

Your pillion needs to be able to reach the footpegs properly and hold onto grab handles or your waist. Legally and practically, they need appropriate protective gear. I won't take anyone on the bike without proper boots, gloves, jacket, trousers, and a decent helmet. It's not worth the risk.

Best UK Roads for Pillion Touring

Some roads suit two-up touring better than others. You want smooth tarmac, flowing corners rather than tight hairpins, and good scenery to make the passenger's experience memorable.

The A82 up the west side of Loch Lomond is brilliant for this – mostly smooth, fantastic views, and the corners are wide enough to maintain good progress without throwing your passenger around. The A591 through the Lake District works well too, particularly the section past Thirlmere.

I avoid really technical roads like some of the Welsh mountain passes when riding two-up. The A5 through Snowdonia is spectacular but quite demanding with a pillion. Save the ultra-technical stuff for solo rides and focus on roads where you can maintain a good flowing rhythm. Check the top 20 motorcycle roads in the UK guide for more specific recommendations.

Building Your First Pillion Tour

Start small. Don't plan a thousand-mile epic for your first two-up tour. I recommend a one or two-day trip with realistic daily mileage – maybe 150-200 miles per day maximum. This gives you both time to adapt without fatigue becoming a major factor.

Use the route builder to plan stops every hour or so. Build in extra time compared to solo riding – everything takes longer with a passenger. Fuel stops, photo stops, meal breaks all expand when you're managing two people's needs.

Choose accommodation carefully. After a day on the bike, your passenger needs proper facilities to refresh and decompress. I've found bike-friendly B&Bs or small hotels work better than camping for first-time pillion tours, though experienced passengers might be fine with camping.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Don't assume your riding style works for passengers. I used to ride quite aggressively solo – that scared the hell out of early pillions. Smooth and predictable beats fast and exciting every time when someone's relying on you.

Don't ignore your passenger's feedback. If they say they're uncomfortable, stop and address it. A numb bum or cramping legs only gets worse with time. I've cut days short because I pushed on when I should've stopped.

Don't forget to adjust your suspension back when you return to solo riding. I've launched off roundabouts a few times because I forgot I still had maximum preload set from two-up riding the previous day.

Making It Enjoyable for Everyone

The best pillion experiences I've had came from treating it as a shared adventure rather than me taking someone along for the ride. Involve your passenger in route planning, stop at places they want to see, and remember they're choosing to spend time on the back of your bike – make it worth their while.

Some of my favourite touring memories involve pillion trips. Watching the sun set over Skye with my partner on the back, stopping at random Highland cafes we'd never have found otherwise, sharing the experience of cresting a hill to see an incredible valley spread out below – these moments are what pillion touring is really about.

The technical challenges are real, and there's definitely a learning curve. But once you've got the basics sorted – proper suspension setup, smooth riding technique, good communication, and regular breaks – two-up touring opens up a whole new dimension of motorcycling. You're sharing something special, and when it works well, it's genuinely magical.

So sort your bike's suspension, brief your passenger properly, plan a modest first route, and get out there. Start with a short day trip somewhere like the Peak District or the North York Moors. Build your confidence and theirs. Before long, you'll be planning proper tours together, and trust me – watching someone you care about experience Britain's incredible roads from the back of your bike is something genuinely special.
